Subscribe The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning Rochester NY at 2:44 p.m. on Saturday for Rochester and nearby Monroe County areas. The warning was set to run until 3:15 p.m. as severe thunderstorms moved through the region. - Advertisement - Rochester and Monroe County The warning covered Rochester, Chili, Le Roy, Byron, Caledonia, Scottsville, Churchville, Riga, Bergen and Elba. Those places were under the same afternoon alert while a flash flood warning for Rochester and several other places was set to last until 7 p.m. By 3 p.m., over 400 RG&E homes in Monroe County were without power. Earlier that day, the largest outage areas at 12:45 p.m. were East Rochester, Pittsford, Perinton and Penfield. Town of Byron storm The National Weather Service said the severe thunderstorm capable of producing a tornado was in the Town of Byron, about seven miles northeast of Batavia, and was moving east at about 35 mph. That placed the warning area beside the storm's path, not just in its center. The Rochester Pride Festival was canceled because of the storms. The Hilton Kiddie Parade was canceled and the Hilton carnival was postponed. - Advertisement - Saturday warning timeline There had also been a tornado warning in the Canandaigua area earlier on Saturday afternoon, and it ended at 1:45 p.m. That warning included Geneva, Canandaigua, Clifton Springs, Phelps, Bloomfield, Farmington, Gorham, East Bloomfield, Manchester and Shortsville. For residents in Rochester and the listed Monroe County communities, the immediate question was whether the warning would end on schedule at 3:15 p.m. or be extended as storms continued to move east. https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: Ukrainian frontline soldiers are alarmed that Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service is reportedly being restricted on fast-moving military platforms, warning of severe operational consequences. “This is comparable to a nuclear strike against us. All operations are on hold. This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. The officer commands a medium-range drone strike unit in southeastern Ukraine. The unit relies heavily on Starlink for the operation and navigation of its American-made Hornet drones, used to strike targets at a range of up to 150 kilometers. Advertisement Advertisement “Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said. POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official. The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company. Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear. The restrictions have brought “all medium-range strike operations to a complete halt,” the officer said, including those using mesh-based systems. These rely on a single Starlink-equipped UAV to receive and relay signals to other drones connected through a mesh network, allowing them to strike targets deep inside Russian-held territory or in areas heavily protected by Russian electronic warfare systems. Such targets include the Donetsk region, the strategically important Novorossiya highway linking Russia to Crimea, the Crimean Peninsula itself, the Kerch area and the Black Sea. Advertisement Advertisement “We can no longer fight effectively to support our infantry on the battlefield. We can no longer strike multiple-launch rocket systems, North Korean-supplied heavy self-propelled artillery positioned deep behind enemy lines, ammunition depots, command centers and other targets,” the officer said. "The Ukrainian frontline is very much dependent on Starlink-operated mid-strike drones," Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian missile-maker Fire Point told POLITICO. Ukraine's devastating campaign For months, Ukrainian medium-range strike drones have inflicted significant damage on Russian logistics in frontline regions. They have disrupted the supply of fuel, ammunition and other military equipment, slowing Russia's advance. The officer said he feared that the Starlink restrictions will give Russian troops a critical opportunity to strengthen their positions. “Starting today, the enemy will build up its logistics routes to Crimea to reinforce its forces there,” he warned. Two other Ukrainian frontline soldiers operating ground robots and conventional first-person-view drones in the Donbas confirmed to POLITICO that Starlink services for Ukrainian units were abruptly restricted on Wednesday. Advertisement Advertisement “On the night of October 14, without prior notice to the Defense Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals while in motion,” a Ukrainian defense ministry official told reporters in Kyiv. The official added that the problems occur at speeds varying from 72 kph to 161 kph, "depending on the specific vehicle and unit." The slowdown in Starlink terminals comes as U.S. President Donald Trump exerts fierce pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries. That follows his deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to release diesel onto global markets — part of Trump’s effort to reduce fuel prices ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said in a Facebook post . Asked about the rising American pressure on Ukraine, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a POLITICO event on Wednesday : "Political development sometimes makes strange influence. Elections are coming." “We are quite dependent on American space capabilities,” Kubilius acknowledged. “The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities.” Advertisement Advertisement The Starlink slowdown was condemned by one of Ukraine’s key European allies. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” wrote Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski. Ukraine depends on Starlink Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Starlink has become central to Kyiv's war effort. In the spring of 2022, Ukrainian defenders trapped in the besieged city of Mariupol used satellites operated by SpaceX to send messages to the outside world. Ukrainian units relied on the system to coordinate operations during the fierce urban fighting around Bakhmut in 2023. To this day, soldiers use Starlink to rapidly adjust artillery fire and navigate naval drones during attacks on Russia's Black Sea Fleet. Ukraine's former army chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, once praised the terminals for their "extraordinary utility." That reliance always carried risk. In the early months of the war, Starlink reportedly shut off terminals that were going to be used in a naval attack on the Russian fleet. But SpaceX has also acted to favor Ukraine. In February, SpaceX shut down access to Starlink terminals being used illegally by Russia, causing immediate chaos. Ukraine then ramped its own use of the terminals. Advertisement Advertisement Kyiv's armed forces began widely equipping medium-range strike drones with Starlink terminals. Without them, operations would become considerably more complex. The military would, for example, have to calculate terrain elevations and antenna availability itself and install additional communications equipment. "Starlink allows you not to have to deal with radio physics," a Ukrainian officer with the call sign Jura said in August. "Starlink allows operators to maintain a live video connection with a drone until shortly before impact." Starlink can also provide so-called "synthetic GPS coordinates," which can help drones navigate when conventional GPS signals are jammed. But Ukrainian officers feared that decisions made in Washington or in the executive offices of American companies could suddenly weaken Ukraine. "Many of my colleagues and I myself are very nervous about the question of how we would operate without Starlink," Jura said. "We have discussed this question several times among our officers: 'What if Elon Musk or someone at SpaceX switches it off?'" As Trump has ramped up pressure on Kyiv in recent weeks, Ukrainian officers reported growing problems with Starlink. Advertisement One Ukrainian drone pilot, who operates medium-range strike drones, reported severe connectivity problems on Sept. 11 and 12, as well as further disruptions on Sept. 17. He said soldiers from several Ukrainian units had experienced similar problems. The incidents occurred shortly after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had concluded visits to Kyiv and Moscow . "After few days, the normal work with Starlink come back. But I believe that was the signal," the pilot said. He argued that Russian jamming equipment could not plausibly have produced such geographically consistent disruptions across multiple sectors of the front. "So that was, I guess, administered from some office," he said. POLITICO could not independently establish whether the disruptions resulted from deliberate restrictions imposed by the American satellite provider or another technical cause. The incidents have reinforced concerns among Ukrainian military personnel about their dependence on American-controlled technology. "The reason is politics and the American option to 'switch off' or critically decrease” U.S. systems, the pilot said. Veronika Melkozerova contributed reporting from Kyiv. Advertisement
